name: South Arete

pitch_detail.notes: The route's short, technical crux: a compact slab pitch with a crack and flake right at the toe of the arete -- by far the shortest pitch but rated the hardest movement on the route.

Scramble right into a gully to a definite chimney, climb it (easy fifth class), then follow broken rock and ledges just south of the ridge crest toward the top; a narrow, exposed crest traverse near the summit is often unprotected.

rappel_detail.pull: Built for a single 60 m rope, and the stations were placed to give steep, clean pulls clear of the gully.
rappel_detail.notes: First of three fixed rappel stations equipped in recent years on the South Arete; single 60m rope is sufficient for each rap.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed bolt/chain station, climber's right of the summer gully/chimney
hazards: One party found one of these bolted stations placed on a large block that is not attached to the mountain: counted from the bottom it is the third, which with three stations in place is this top one, above the gully. Inspect the rock the bolts are in, not only the hardware, and back it up if you are not satisfied.
The short 5th-class step above the station is exposed with real fall consequence. Stay roped, and place gear on it rather than soloing down.
rappel_detail.station: Top station of the rappel line North Cascade Mountain Guides installed after the June 2022 rockfall: bolts and chains on a big ledge immediately above the small tree that older parties used to sling. All three new stations sit climber's right of the gully and off the line of ascent — skier's left as you face out on the way down — deliberately taking the descent out of the gully feature the route climbs. You reach it by downclimbing the arete's 3rd/4th-class ground plus one short, exposed 5th-class step.

rappel_detail.pull: Steep and fairly clean on a 60 m rope, provided the strands are kept out of the gully when you throw.
rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the arete; short easy downclimbing sections connect stations.
hazards: The gully immediately beside the line is the loose ground that produced the 2022 rockfall. Keep ropes and feet out of it — that is the whole reason this rappel line was moved.
This is a very popular route and stations back up on summer weekends; anything knocked loose lands on the party waiting below.
rappel_detail.station: Second of the three chain-and-bolt stations, on the ledge just above the chockstone, again set off to the side of the climbing line. Short sections of easy downclimbing link it to the station above, and how much you rappel versus downclimb is a party choice.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel returns to the base of the route.
hazards: Talus and slabs immediately below the last station, with the pull zone directly above anyone still coiling ropes.

The alternative descent some parties take instead — traversing to the Southwest Couloir and walking it out — avoids rope work but is loose and can hold firm snow well into summer, so it is not automatically the safer option without an axe.
rappel_detail.station: Lowest chain station. The rappel from it returns you to the base of the route, where the climbers' trail leads back down through talus and slabs alongside the stream to the Blue Lake Trail.

rappels: 3 single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted chain anchors on the South Arete descent, each under 30 m, with easy downclimbing between them
descent_text: Descend by rappelling/downclimbing the South Arete climbing route itself. In recent years the route has been equipped with three fixed rappel stations (bolts and chains) set slightly climber's right of the summer gully/chimney and off the main line of ascent, giving clean, mostly-vertical pulls; a single 60m rope is sufficient for each rappel and gets you back to the base of the route in 2-3 rappels, supplemented by short sections of easy downclimbing between stations depending on how much you choose to downclimb versus rappel. Because some of the down-climbing is exposed with real fall consequences, parties newer to alpine terrain should stay roped and consider placing gear on the downclimbed sections rather than soloing them. From the base of the raps, reverse the approach: pick up the climbers' trail back down through the talus and slabs paralleling the stream to the Blue Lake Trail, then follow it back to the trailhead. An alternative descent used by some parties is to traverse to the Southwest Couloir and downclimb/walk that gully back into the basin instead of re-rapping the arete; it avoids rope work but is loose underfoot and can hold firm snow well into summer, in which case an ice axe (and possibly crampons) is warranted.
approach: Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (elev. ~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the well-built Blue Lake Trail (Trail #314) as it climbs gently through subalpine fir and larch forest, switchbacking up open slabs with good views back at the highway. After roughly 1.3-1.5 miles and about 1,000 ft of gain, watch for a minor stream crossing/drainage coming down from the basin below the Early Winter Spires — this is well before Blue Lake itself, which lies another mile-plus further on the maintained trail. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the climbers' boot path (cairned but braided in spots) that works up through granite slabs and heather benches, then continues up open talus and boulder country roughly parallel to the stream, which is a reliable water source through most of the season lower down but disappears into talus higher up — fill up before leaving it. Continue up this climbers' trail, angling toward the southwestern corner/toe of South Early Winter Spire (the right-hand, southernmost of the two spires, before the saddle). Expect roughly another 1,000 ft of gain from where you leave the maintained trail to reach the base of the route at the level of the North/South spire saddle, for a total of about 2.5 hours and up to ~2,000 ft of gain from the car. The path is mostly straightforward but loses definition on the upper talus and slab benches — trend toward the obvious southwest corner of the spire rather than chasing any single cairn line, and take care on the granite slabs low down when wet or covered in old snow, which can persist into early summer in shaded gullies.
overview: The standard, most-climbed route on South Early Winters Spire and the second most popular route in the Liberty Bell Group after the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell — a short, moderate outing well suited to parties wanting the summit with minimal commitment. First ascended by Fred and Helmy Beckey, June 1942.
beta: From the base, pitch 1 climbs a short steep crack; then either go right and up (5.5, stretching across a slab) to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab (5.5 finger traverse), then easy climbing to a belay beneath the whitish south corner splitting the arete. Pitch 2 climbs a gully that becomes a chockstone chimney for about 100 feet with one 5.4 move in the chimney, then easier ground leads to the summit.
fa: Fred Beckey and Helmy Beckey, June 19, 1942
